newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Be patient, Mandela urges cold, wet S.Africans.
newsitem.headline: Be patient, Mandela urges cold, wet S.Africans.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela on Wednesday urged South African shack dwellers shivering through a cold, wet winter to be patient in waiting for proper houses and services which he acknowledged were slow in coming.
"What the people of this country want, is not speeches... they want houses, they want electricity," Mandela told destitute blacks in a ramshackle slum bearing his name in Cape Town's Hout Bay suburb.
Mandela was touring squatter settlements, most built from scavenged planks and sheet metal, where scores of shacks have been flattened in recent days by winter storms.
"There is naturally impatience on the part of our people, impatience which is understandable...after we have been in government for three years," he said.
"It is understandable that people should ask, 'what has the government been doing over these three years?'," Mandela said.
He reminded his audience that in the run-up to South Africa's first all-race elections in 1994 he had warned supporters against expecting too much too soon from a black majority government.

"This process is going to take even as long as five years before you can actually see delivery of basic services.... We have inherited a debt from the previous apartheid regime of 250 billion rand($55.2 billion)," Mandela said.
This financial burden meant his government could not deliver quickly on its promises of basic services.
Mandela said that it was not enough for people whose shacks had been blown down in storms to tell them about food feeding schemes in other parts of the country.
"I would appeal to you again to be patient. You have got a government that cares," he said.
"In spite of all the plans we have been making, we have barely touched the surface of the problems relating to housing, education, health and so on, but our intention is to deliver...
"I would rather you stoned me, rather than make false promises. I am not bringing you houses today, I am saying this is a process and it is going to take quite some time."
Mandela's African National Congress government promised when taking office to build a million houses for the poor within five years, but appears to be some way from meeting the target.
It faces its next election in 1999, when Mandela is due to retire from politics. ($ = 4.529 South African Rand)
